name: Rugged individualism
summary: Rugged individualism is the American doctrine Herbert Hoover named in 1928: progress comes from individual initiative and enterprise, equal opportunity and decentralized local self-government. Government acts as umpire, regulating monopoly and public utilities, but must stay out of running business, and hardship is met first by voluntary charity, mutual self-help and local government. Hoover insists it is not laissez faire and that it rejects both socialism and class domination.
scope: The doctrine as stated by Herbert Hoover, who used the phrase 'the American system of rugged individualism' in his 22 October 1928 speech (s2, s4) and elaborated it in American Individualism (1922, s3); the Yale teaching unit (s1) identifies the phrase with his view of government and business. It does not include Hoover's tariff, foreign, Prohibition or other policy beyond these texts, nor the later polemical use of the phrase for pure self-reliance or atomism, which Hoover's texts reject.
